1.pericope_label: The butler and baker offend and are put in ward with Joseph

schools.summary: Calvin insists we are not to understand any common person of each rank, but those who presided over the rest, since they are soon afterwards called eunuchs or nobles: they were, in short, two of the chief men of the court. He takes the identification of the captain of the guard with Potiphar as evidence that Potiphar's anger had by now been mitigated, since without his consent the jailer could never have treated Joseph with such clemency; and he sets the whole episode in the frame of providence, noting that God, before he opened the door for his servant's deliverance, entered the very prison to sustain him, and afterwards chose to lead him around by circuitous paths rather than deliver him directly, the better to prove his patience and to show that he has wonderful methods of working hidden from our view. Gill notes that the captain of the guard in whose house they were confined is generally thought to be Potiphar himself, unless he had died and another was put into his room, and supposes Joseph was recommended to him by the keeper of the prison for his prudence and fidelity; he adds that some render the clause the other way, that he committed Joseph to be with them, as Jarchi interprets it, the three being put together not merely for company but that Joseph might wait upon them.

Henry begins by asking why the story is in scripture at all, and answers that we should not have had this account of Pharaoh's butler and baker recorded if it had not been serviceable to Joseph's preferment, for the world stands for the sake of the church and is governed for its good. From the fall of the two officers he draws his moral — high places are slippery places, and nothing is more uncertain than the favour of princes, whereas those who make God's favour their happiness will find him a better Master than Pharaoh, and not so extreme to mark what they do amiss. Of their offence he reports the conjectures without choosing among them: some make it no less than an attempt to take away the king's life, others no more than the casual lighting of a fly into his cup and a little sand into his bread; whatever it was, Providence by this means brought them into the prison where Joseph was. That the captain of the guard charged Joseph with them he reads as the first thaw, intimating that Potiphar began now to be reconciled to him and perhaps to be convinced of his innocence, though he durst not release him for fear of disobliging his wife — John Baptist must lose his head to please Herodias. Wesley reproduces the opening of this comment almost word for word, and adds only that the charge intimates Potiphar was becoming reconciled to Joseph.

Clarke inclines to the graver conjecture about the offence, that the two had probably been accused of attempting the king's life, the one by poisoning his drink and the other his bread. He gives the words behind the offices, the butler being a cup-bearer, the same as the saky among the Arabians and Persians, and the baker rather a cook or confectioner, and explains why such men went to that particular prison: according to Diodorus every officer of the ancient kings of Egypt was drawn from the most illustrious priestly families, no common person being permitted to serve in the king's presence, so that men of noble family, when accused, went naturally to the state prison. Of the length of their confinement he observes that the word is literally days, that many suppose a complete year, and that Calmet, reckoning back from Pharaoh's birthday, supposed they had offended on the preceding one.

Ellicott adds, out of Wilkinson's work on the monuments, that the Egyptians had carried the art of making confectionery to very great perfection. Keil marks what the interval in prison ended in: after some time, and on the same night, these two prisoners each had a dream of his own, each one answering to the interpretation which specially applied to him.

debates.question: What was the offence of the butler and the baker?

positions.position: unknown; the conjectures run from an attempt on the king's life to a fly in his cup and sand in his bread
probably an accusation of attempting the king's life, by poisoning his drink and his bread

outliers.note: reads the whole imprisonment as method rather than delay, God choosing to lead Joseph around by circuitous paths instead of delivering him directly, the better to prove his patience

themes: what the two officers had done
their rank and the prison they went to

5.pericope_label: The two dreams, and Joseph's claim that interpretation is God's

schools.summary: Gill notes first that it was not one dream between them but a dream apiece, and that Joseph and they were in the same prison but not the same ward, Joseph coming in each morning like a careful and faithful servant to see that the prisoners in his charge were safe and to learn what they wanted. Calvin argues from the men's own reaction that these dreams were of the prophetic kind: many frivolous things are presented to us which pass away and are forgotten, but some have the force and significance of prophecy, and unless the mark of a celestial oracle had been engraven upon these, the butler and the baker would never have fallen into such consternation of mind — men are sometimes agitated by vain dreams, he grants, but there the terror subsides, whereas here God had fixed an arrow in their minds which would not suffer them to rest. He turns the compassion Joseph showed back on the reader, since men are softened by their own afflictions so that they do not despise others in misery, and such humanity has to be learned by experience. Calvin also dates Joseph's gift precisely: by a new inspiration of the Spirit the power of prophecy, which he had not before possessed, was imparted to him in the prison, so that where he had once remained in suspense about his own dreams he is now a certain interpreter to others. Yet he claims nothing peculiar to God, offering his service only so far as his calling supplies the means; and Calvin contrasts Daniel, who by a larger measure of the Spirit could both recover a forgotten dream and expound it, with Joseph, to whom the half only of these gifts was given, who does not divine what they dreamed but confesses that it is hidden from him.

Henry ascribes the two dreams to a special providence which filled the heads of these prisoners with unusual dreams carrying evidences of a divine origin, and adds that God has immediate access to the spirits of men and can make them serviceable to his own purposes quite beyond the intention of those concerned. Of their sadness he says, in a sentence Wesley reproduces almost word for word, that it was not the prison that made them sad, for they were pretty well used to that and perhaps lived jovially enough there, but the dream: God has more ways than one to sadden the spirits of those that are to be made sad, and sinners hardy enough under outward troubles he can still reach by wounding their spirits. He makes much of Joseph's conduct that morning — he was their keeper, and in that office he was mild; it becomes us to take cognizance of the sorrows even of those under our check, and it is some relief to men in trouble to be noticed; he was their companion in tribulation too, and communion in sufferings works compassion.

Clarke marks the difference from ordinary dreaming, the disordered working of a mind disturbed by disease or repletion, whereas these had an interpretation, that is, were prophetic; and of the prisoners' complaint he says they either had access to no interpreter or got no satisfactory meaning from those they asked. God alone, he adds, knows what is in futurity, and if he has sent a significant dream he alone can give the solution.

Ellicott is more precise about why no interpreter was to be had: in Egypt the interpreting of dreams was the business of trained men, the magicians and wise men of the next chapter, and to such the prisoners could have no access from their prison — though Joseph denies that art and training can avail at all, and claims the interpretation for God. Keil reads Joseph's answer as a double move, since he reminded them first that interpretations are God's and his gift, and then bade them tell him their dreams, from a consciousness, no doubt, that he was himself endowed with that gift.

debates.question: How do these dreams differ from ordinary dreaming?

positions.position: ordinary dreams are the disordered working of a mind disturbed by disease or repletion; these had an interpretation, that is, were prophetic
the men's own consternation proves it, since vain dreams lose their terror but God had fixed an arrow in these minds that would not let them rest
a special providence filled their heads with dreams carrying evidence of a divine origin, God having immediate access to the spirits of men

outliers.note: measures Joseph's gift against Daniel's and finds it half as large, since Daniel could recover a forgotten dream as well as expound it, whereas Joseph must confess that what they dreamed is hidden from him

themes: two prophetic dreams in one night
why the dreams made them sad
do not interpretations belong to God

9.pericope_label: The butler's dream interpreted, and Joseph's request

schools.summary: Gill notes that the butler was forward to speak first, whereas the baker held back until he saw what a good interpretation the first dream received. On Joseph's request to be remembered he reports the charge made against him in the Targum's words, that Joseph lost his superior confidence and retained the confidence of men, and answers that means are always to be used in subordination to the divine will. Calvin insists that Joseph does not offer what he thought probable, like some ambiguous conjecturer, but asserts the meaning by the revelation of the Spirit — for why say that the three branches are three days rather than anything else, unless the Spirit had suggested it? — and that by commending himself to the butler at once, as if the man were already restored, he shows how indubitable he held his own reading to be. He meets the objection that Joseph sought a reward for prophecy: he did not set the gift of God to sale, but saw that a method of deliverance was now set before him by God which it was not lawful to refuse, since God, who from his childhood had twice promised him dominion, had not left him amid so many straits without consolation.

Clarke takes the dream as evidence that wine anciently was the mere expressed juice of the grape without fermentation, the cup-bearer taking the bunch, pressing the juice into the cup and instantly delivering it to his master. He also seizes on the little word are in the interpretation, which here means signify: so this is my body means this bread represents my body, a form of speech frequent in scripture because the Hebrew has no proper word for signifies or represents. Wesley, in words Henry had used before him, admires the modesty of Joseph's account of himself: he does not reflect upon the brothers who sold him, saying only that he was stolen out of the land of the Hebrews, nor upon the mistress who persecuted him or the master who judged him, but mildly avers his own innocence — and when we are called to vindicate ourselves we should carefully avoid speaking ill of others.

Ellicott reaches a middle position on the wine from the other side: Plutarch's claim that before Psammetichus the Egyptians neither drank wine nor poured it out to the gods has been abundantly disproved, and probably arose from taking the custom of one district for the universal rule; nevertheless the king's drink here does not look like fermented wine but like a sort of sherbet of fresh grape-juice and water. He finds a second Egyptian fingerprint in the dream's last words, since the Hebrew says not into Pharaoh's hand but upon Pharaoh's palm, the hollow made by bending the fingers inwards: where the Hebrews always spoke of placing a cup in a man's hand, as Joseph himself does a verse later, the Egyptian cup-bearer uses the idiom of his own country, Egyptian cups having no stems but being flat bowls held in the very way he describes. Of Joseph's reticence about his brothers he offers a further reason, that his purpose was to rouse the Egyptian's sympathy by letting him know he was free born and reduced to slavery by fraud, whereas to have said his sale was owing to family feuds would have done harm rather than good, and noble-minded men do not willingly reveal what is to the discredit of their relatives. Keil warns against forcing the dream's detail so far as to prove that the kings of Egypt drank only fresh juice, since the cultivation of the vine and the drinking of wine among the Egyptians are established beyond question by ancient testimony and the earliest monuments, whatever Herodotus said.

debates.question: Was the drink the butler prepared fermented wine?

positions.position: no; the dream shows that ancient wine was the mere expressed juice of the grape, pressed into the cup and delivered at once
the detail must not be forced so far, since the making and drinking of wine in Egypt is established beyond question by the monuments
wine certainly existed in Egypt, but the king's drink here looks rather like a sherbet of fresh grape-juice and water

debates.question: Was Joseph wrong to ask the butler's help?

positions.position: the Targum charges him with losing his confidence in God and retaining the confidence of men, but means are to be used in subordination to the divine will
no; the opportunity was set before him by God and could not lawfully be refused, and he did not set the gift of God to sale

outliers.note: detects the narrator's Egyptian knowledge in an idiom, since the cup-bearer speaks of the cup upon Pharaoh's palm where a Hebrew would say in his hand — Egyptian cups being stemless bowls

themes: whether the king drank fermented wine
why Joseph asked to be remembered

16.pericope_label: The baker's dream and the sentence upon him

schools.summary: Gill is careful about what the baker saw: the interpretation was good, meaning not that it was right and just, though it was, but that it was agreeable and pleasing and portended well in the event, and it was that which drew the second dream out of a man who might otherwise have kept it to himself. Of the dream he notes that the bakemeats were all sorts of pastry, tarts and pies and the like, and reports from Josephus that two of the baskets were full of bread while the third held the various kinds of food usually prepared for kings; and he observes that Joseph answered immediately, without any further thought or meditation, being divinely instructed. On the sentence he gives the Targum's blunt paraphrase, that Pharaoh should remove the man's head from his body with a sword. Calvin turns the baker's motive into a warning, since he does not care about Joseph's skill and fidelity as an interpreter but desires an interpretation only because Joseph had brought good tidings to his companion — so many desire the word of God with ardour and alacrity, not because they wish to be governed by the Lord and to know what is right, but because they dream of mere enjoyment, and when the doctrine does not correspond with their wishes they depart sorrowful and wounded. Calvin presses hardest on Joseph's freedom of speech: though the explanation was about to prove unpleasant and severe, he declared without ambiguity what had been revealed to him and so executed with fidelity the office divinely committed to him, and this freedom must be maintained by prophets and teachers, that they may not hesitate to inflict a wound by their teaching upon those whom God has sentenced to death. All love to be flattered, and the majority of teachers, wishing to yield to the corrupt wishes of the world, adulterate the word of God. He also notes what the double fulfilment established, that when Moses relates that what Joseph foretold happened to both men he proves by that sign that Joseph was a true prophet of God — for though the prophets sometimes threatened punishments which God then abstained from inflicting, that was because a condition was annexed to such prophecies, whereas when the Lord speaks positively by his servants, whatever he predicts must be confirmed by the result. On the ambiguous phrase itself Calvin observes that by itself it may be taken in a good sense or a bad, so that the added words carry the whole weight: there seems to be an allusion of this kind, as if Joseph had said, Pharaoh will lift up thy head, that he may take it off.

Clarke supplies the practice behind the sentence, that beheading, hanging and gibbeting were all modes of punishment among the ancient Egyptians, the criminal being beheaded first and then hung either on hooks or by the hands.

Ellicott puts the difference between the two sentences plainly: a few verses earlier the lifting up of the butler's head meant his elevation to his former rank, whereas here the significant addition from off thee implies that he would be beheaded and his body publicly exposed to ignominy. Keil observes that the carrying of the baskets upon the head is thoroughly Egyptian, and cites Herodotus for it.

debates.question: What does lifting up the head mean in the baker's case?

positions.position: the phrase is ambiguous by itself and the added words carry the weight — Pharaoh will lift up thy head, that he may take it off
the addition from off thee implies beheading, and the body publicly exposed to ignominy

outliers.note: draws a rule for preachers out of Joseph's plain speaking, that no one is a sincere minister of God's word but he who, despising reproach, frames his teaching by God's command rather than by the wishes of those who love to be flattered

themes: why the baker told his dream
the freedom of an interpreter who must wound
lifting up the head from off him

20.pericope_label: Pharaoh's birthday, the two fates, and the butler's forgetting

schools.summary: Gill pauses over what kind of birthday is meant, since the word could cover either the king's natural birth or the anniversary of his accession, and judges the natural birthday likelier, that being the Egyptian custom as it was the Persian. Of the forgetting he notes that the butler said nothing that day nor for two years after, and calls it great ingratitude and the frequent character of courtiers, who in high places neglect both the petitions made to them and their own promises. Calvin will not condemn the keeping of birthdays either, if only men would keep the right end in view and give thanks to God by whom they were created; but the world distorts what the fathers honestly instituted, so that most keep up the memory of God as the Author of their life as if their set purpose were to forget him. He adds a shrewder reason for the butler's silence than mere forgetfulness, that the man did not dare mention Joseph lest he bring reproach on himself or trouble the king, since it is common with courtiers perfidiously to betray the innocent rather than offend those they are afraid of; and he finds the delay purposeful, teaching us that nothing is more improper than to prescribe the time in which God shall help us — had liberty come by the butler's entreaty, the benefit would have been credited to man and not to God.

Henry allows the keeping of birthdays provided it is not abused as Jeroboam's and Herod's were, and turns it to use: we may all profitably take notice of our birthdays, with thankfulness for the mercies of our birth, sorrow for the sinfulness of it, and an expectation of the day of our death as better than the day of our birth. He draws the moral of the speed of the reversal, both men being advanced at the three days' end, the one to his office and the other to the gallows, so sudden are the revolutions of the wheel of nature. He then reports with approval the old parallel between Joseph and Christ — Joseph's two fellow-prisoners answering to the two thieves crucified with Christ, one saved and one condemned, and the butler forgetting the man who said remember me, where the thief who said remember me was not forgotten.

Clarke thinks the keeping of birthdays with a feast very ancient, and guesses it arose from a correct notion of the immortality of the soul, the commencement of life appearing of great consequence to one who believed he was to live for ever. He takes the lifting up of the two heads to mean bringing them to trial, comparing the trial of Naboth, who was set on high among the people before the witnesses were produced, the issue being that the baker alone was found guilty while the butler was acquitted and restored; Wesley reads the phrase the same way, as arraigned and tried them. On the typology Clarke breaks with Henry entirely. Many commentators, he says, have seen in every circumstance of Joseph's history a parallel to our blessed Lord, and he believes God never designed such parallels; he is astonished to find grave and judicious men forcing the features of truth into so distorted a shape, warns against attributing to God designs he never had, and holds the mischief of this system to be really incalculable, since it gives the irreligious a pretext to scoff at all spirituality. He notes too that had the butler mentioned the circumstance to Pharaoh, Joseph's case would have been examined into and he would have been restored to liberty.

Ellicott thinks the phrase about lifting up the head is more probably used to point out the exact fulfilment of Joseph's interpretation of the two dreams than to describe a trial. Keil simply records the double outcome, that Pharaoh lifted up the heads of both prisoners but in very different ways, the cup-bearer being pardoned and reinstated in his office and the baker executed, and that the butler then forgot Joseph in his prosperity and did nothing to procure his liberation.

more probably it points out the exact fulfilment of Joseph's interpretation of the two dreams
